subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Oh-My-God Particle
description: A quick, practical guide to The Oh-My-God Particle.

hook.text: In 1991, a cosmic ray hit Utah carrying the energy of a fast baseball—in a single proton. They called it the Oh-My-God particle.

buildup.text: Its energy was 300 million trillion electronvolts—far beyond anything a human-built accelerator has ever achieved.

discovery.text: The Fly's Eye detector measured it. At that energy, the proton was traveling at 99.99999999999999999999951% the speed of light.

twist.text: Physics says such particles should lose energy hitting microwave background photons. How this one survived the trip is unclear.

climax.text: Its source is unknown. No known mechanism easily explains how a single proton reaches such extreme energy.

punchline.text: One proton, baseball energy. We still don't know what launched it.

quiz.question: Why is the Oh-My-God particle scientifically puzzling?
options: Its extreme energy should have been lost during travel, and its source is unknown
It was the first particle ever detected from outside our galaxy
It traveled faster than light, violating Einstein's theory of relativity

details.summary: The Oh-My-God particle was an ultra-high-energy cosmic ray detected in Utah in 1991, carrying an energy of 3×10²⁰ eV — equivalent to a baseball pitched at 60 mph compressed into a single proton. Its energy exceeded theoretical limits, and its source remains unknown decades later.
details.whyItMatters: The Oh-My-God particle challenges our understanding of cosmic ray physics. Its energy exceeded the GZK limit, raising questions about what natural accelerator could produce such extreme particles.
takeaways: A cosmic ray with the kinetic energy of a fast baseball
Detected in 1991 with energy exceeding theoretical limits
Its source and acceleration mechanism remain unknown

faq.question: What is the GZK limit and why did this particle violate it?
faq.answer: The GZK (Greisen-Zatsepin-Kuzmin) limit predicts that cosmic rays above ~5×10¹⁹ eV should lose energy interacting with the cosmic microwave background during transit. The Oh-My-God particle exceeded this, implying either a nearby source, new physics, or extreme conditions not yet understood.

faq.question: Have more ultra-high-energy cosmic rays been detected since?
faq.answer: Yes. The Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina and the Telescope Array in Utah have detected many particles approaching similar energies. In 2021, the Amaterasu particle was detected at 2.4×10²⁰ eV, coming from a direction with no obvious source. The mystery persists.
